source: SPLYT’s in-app What’s New screen (Profile → Tools → What’s New), copied from SPLYT’s codebase. It lists every build, including over-the-air updates that never appear as an App Store release.

coverage.note: Only entries inside the scoreboard window are published here. Only the "new" section is counted; "improved" and "fixed" items are counted but not listed.

new: A weight screen in Food: your weight against what you ate each day and your calorie goal, over 4 weeks, 3 months or a year. Log today’s weight right there.
Build your meal plan by saying it, snapping a photo, picking a file or pasting it in. Check the meals it found, then add them in one go.

Food log. Type or say what you ate, the way you’d text a friend, and Splyt counts the calories, protein, fat and carbs. Several meals in one message land in their own places, and “at 9 am” puts it at 9.
Your nutrition goal. Pick lose fat, maintain or build muscle, and Splyt works out your targets from your profile (and shows the math), or enter your own.
Meal plans. Add the meals you eat most days at their times. They count by themselves once their time passes, unless you say you missed one or had something else.
Missed a meal? Ask what you can eat instead and pick one of the ideas, or type what you had. It changes today only.
A meal calendar, styled like your training calendar, and you can see your friends’ meals too.
Splyt AI knows what you’ve eaten and what’s on your plan, so its advice fits your day.
Tap any photo in your check-in to see it full screen. Swipe through the set, pinch to zoom in, and retake one right from there.
Finish a check-in early: once you’ve taken a photo, tap Finish to save just the ones you have.
A fresh look for the voice button in a workout. The first time you tap it, a short intro plays real examples of what you can say.
While you talk, your words appear above the button as you say them. Afterwards it tells you exactly what changed — “Set 3 → 135 lbs · Warm-up set added” — with Undo, and the sets it touched light up.
Say it loosely: “swap my dumbbell shoulder movement for an overhead press, three sets” just works. If it really can’t tell which one you mean, it asks, and you tap the answer.
Your weekly recap now opens as a card the first time you open the app in a new week, with your day rings filling in.
Start a workout with Siri on your phone or watch — “start today’s workout in Splyt” or “start a run in Splyt”. On your watch, a template’s name works too.
A new look for Notifications: coloured icons, search, and a filter menu. Unread stays unread until you open it.
A new look for My Splits, with a + to start a new one.
Talk to the progress photo camera like a person. “Wait, can we redo the last one”, “show me how to do this one”, “turn your mic off”, “why aren’t you taking it?” — it answers out loud and does it.
The camera’s mic has its own button: tap it to stop or start listening.
Voice logging shows your words as you say them, punctuated and with gym words spelled right, then double-checks the whole take before reading it.
Compare side by side now shows the whole photo — arms and all. Pinch to zoom and drag; both photos move together. Double-tap to zoom in or back out.
See your future has its own button on Compare, next to Share.
Fix a photo filed under the wrong pose: tap the pose name under the date and pick the right one.
A reminder the day before your split ends, and a nudge the morning after if you haven’t picked what’s next.
A fresh Liquid Glass look: back, close and header buttons across the app are now glass.
Start a workout from your Lock Screen: add the Splyt start button and you’re one tap from an empty session.
Log cardio by voice: say “30 minutes on the StairMaster, level 7, heart rate 150” and it’s saved as that activity, with its time, heart rate and calories.
Two new buttons on Home: Empty workout starts a blank session, and Template starts one of your saved workouts.

Progress photos has a Relaxed mode for lining up: it accepts a little less precision and gives up sooner when you just want the photo. Say “take it” twice in a check-in and it switches to Relaxed on its own.
Ask Claude or ChatGPT about your training. Profile → Claude & ChatGPT walks you through connecting Splyt in a minute — it can read your workouts, PRs and progress, and never changes anything.
Rate Splyt from Profile: one tap opens our App Store page, ready for your review.
Group chats have a menu: turn on Hide Alerts, or leave the chat.
Home View now also sits under Account on the You tab.
Progress photos, redesigned. Your latest check-in fills the screen — drag the timeline to go back in time, hold the photo to compare with today, or press play to watch one pose change.

A guided check-in that can see you. Prop your phone up and step back: Splyt waits until your phone is set down and straight, the light is right, all of you is in frame and you’re in the pose — then counts down. Move during the countdown and it stops and tells you why.
Talk to the camera from across the room: say “wait”, “go”, “take it”, “redo that”, “skip”, “what’s next” or “I’m done”.
Short on space? Frame from your knees up instead of head to toe — the coach offers it when you can’t step back any further.
Each new pose shows large for a moment so you can see what to do, then tucks into the corner.
Every pose guide is now a photo of someone doing the pose — a man or a woman, to match you — instead of a drawing.
The camera remembers whether you use the front or back camera. Double-tap to switch.
Compare like a camera: swipe between Slide, Fade, Side by side, All poses and Future.
Share a before-and-after with your face hidden, and see your whole journey wipe from day one to today after each check-in.
Make a pose of your own by posing a figure — it becomes the outline you line up with.
Bring in up to 40 old photos at once. Splyt dates and sorts them, and you swipe to confirm the ones it isn’t sure of.
Missed a pose? Tap Add at the end of today’s poses to take just that one.
Compare shows what you weighed on both dates, as well as the change.
Play runs once from your first check-in to today, lined up on you so you stay in place — no jumping between photos.
Every check-in in the grid is framed on you rather than the room, and shows its date.
Splyt AI checks in when your week starts: why a session was missed, whether today’s plan is on, and whether to make it up. (Pro)
Missed workouts get their own card. Catch up with just the key lifts, or the whole session, and see exactly what’s in it first.
Chat with your trainer like Messages: react, reply to a message, edit or unsend, and see when it’s been read.
Trainers: see every missed session, whether it was made up, and a follow-up drafted for clients who’ve gone quiet.
See your future: your progress photo, 1, 3, 6 or 12 months from now, based on your own weigh-ins and how often you actually train. Drag to compare. Find it under Progress photos → ⋯. (Pro)
Search your progress photos and ask Splyt AI about them, right from the Progress photos screen.

Splyt speaks your language. Dates, numbers, kg and km now follow your phone, exercise search understands Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, German and French, and the import flow is translated into all five. Change it any time in Profile → Language.
Identify a machine: snap any gym machine and Splyt tells you what it is and adds the exercise to your workout (Pro).
Chat with the founders like you text a friend: replies, reactions, and typing.
Workout Settings: your rest timer, sets and reps, weight auto-fill, workout layout and screen lock, each on a short page of its own. Find it in Settings or on the You tab.
Workout Save Reminder: choose when Splyt reminds you to finish a workout — after a set time with nothing logged, or as soon as you leave the gym.
See whether your watch is synced: a quick note each time you open Splyt, and your watch’s status in Settings and Wearables.
Short videos explain auto rep tracking, the rest timer and the live workout screen.
iPhone Duo: unfold it and Splyt uses the whole screen — a sidebar for your tabs, your exercises beside your sets mid-workout, and two-column exercise and workout pages.
Missed a split day? Home offers to catch up — just the 3 key lifts, or the full workout — and starts it in one tap. You can switch between the two any time, and it works on splyt.fit too.
Wearables: Profile → Connected shows what Splyt works with and what’s coming next. Want Garmin, or something else you wear? Tap “I want this” or type it in — we build what people ask for most.
Steps: tap Steps on Home, then the avatar next to the title, to see how a friend's day is going hour by hour — their pace, their usual day, and their week.
A Splyt widget for your Home Screen and Lock Screen with your rings and today’s workout.
A Splyt control for Control Center, the Lock Screen and the Action button: start a workout in one press.

A new Splyt widget for your Home Screen and Lock Screen: your rings and today’s workout — and with POTS mode on, your heart, how today looks, your fluids with a +250 button, or “I need you”. Hold it and tap Edit Widget to choose.

A Splyt control for the Lock Screen, Control Center and the Action button. Start a workout — and with POTS mode on: I need you, Settle, +250 ml, +1 g salt, I’m okay or Stand test. Press and hold I need you on your Lock Screen to tell your person without unlocking.
While you settle, your Lock Screen and Dynamic Island show how long it’s been and whether your person has seen it or is on the way.
For the person who has your back: a widget that shows how they’re doing (only what they share), and when they need you, “On my way” right from it.
POTS mode has a new setup: set where high starts for you on your own heart line, drag your daily fluids into a tank, and choose exactly what your person sees.
For the person who has your back: a new welcome that walks through what you share, how alerts reach them, and the ways to help — from your own plan.

POTS mode: the people you share with can add what they noticed — “Looked pale”, “Went quiet”. It shows under your episodes, and you can put it in your doctor report. They can’t change anything of yours.
On Apple Watch (beta, off unless you turn it on): if it looks like you might have fainted, your watch asks if you’re okay — and tells your people if you don’t answer.
POTS mode: My plan — tell your people how it starts for you, what helps, what not to do and when to call 911. They see it the moment you need them.
POTS mode: Check on me — about to shower or lie down alone? Start a timer. If you don’t check in, your person is told.
POTS mode: your meds with times, and gentle reminders you can mark Taken or snooze right from the notification.
POTS mode: every episode in one list. Add what happened whenever you’re up to it, or log a rough moment in one tap.
POTS mode: show your heart as a feeling — Steady, Rising, High — instead of a number. Turn it on in POTS settings.
POTS mode: an optional heads-up on hot days, from today’s forecast where you are.
POTS mode: log any amount, salt in grams or milligrams of sodium, and electrolyte drinks — they count toward fluids and salt.
A fluids widget for your Home Screen and Lock Screen, with a +250 button.
On Apple Watch: pour fluids with the Digital Crown.
POTS mode: a full-screen Fluids view — drag up to pour, and see where you are against your pace for the day.
POTS mode: when your heart is running high, pull the orb down to start settling.

POTS mode. If you live with POTS, turn it on in You → POTS mode and Home becomes your day: how you feel in one tap, fluids and salt, what your heart is doing, and a daily outlook once Splyt knows your usual. It’s free.

“I need you” — one tap tells the people you choose to come, to call, or just that it’s a rough moment, even when you can’t explain. You see the moment they’ve seen it and what they said back. Your Apple Watch has it too.
Heart alerts from your watch when your heart runs high and stays there — sent to your people only if you say so, and only after asking you first unless you turn that off.

Supporting someone with POTS: accept their invite and their day shows at the top of your Home — a word, never the details. Alerts reach you even when you’re busy, with On my way, I’ll call and Got it right on the notification.
A guided stand test, a calm-down coach for when it hits, a six-stage reconditioning plan with a heart-rate ceiling on your watch, and a two-page report for your doctor.

Progress photos are organised as check-ins now, not a wall of tiles. One card per session with the week number and what you weighed, the first and latest shot side by side at the top with the weeks and pounds between them, and a compare view you can wipe one photo across the other. There are eleven poses instead of four — relaxed and flexed — and you can name your own. Tap the eye to blur every thumbnail when you’re not somewhere private.

Measurements. A tape measure catches what the scale misses, so Body now tracks your waist, hips, chest, shoulders, arms and the rest alongside your weight — with body fat if you log it. Measure in a guided check-in that asks for one number at a time, slide to the reading instead of typing it, and see how each one has moved since you started. Waist-to-hip and waist-to-height are worked out for you. Find it under Your progress on the You tab.
Your progress on the You tab now shows where you actually are — your waist since you started, with a trend line, and your most recent photo — rather than describing what the feature does.

Setting yourself up to coach is a guided flow now, in three parts: about you, how clients work with you, and your public page. The middle part is the new one — your intake form, how often check-ins land and what fills itself in, what people can book and your hours. All of it is the starting point for everyone who joins you, and the last step reads your whole flow back to you with sketches of the five screens a new client actually meets.
Trainers: a half-finished setup is findable again. You and Coach both offer to pick it up where you left off.

Trainers: the intake your new clients fill in is yours now. Edit the questions, bring the intake you already use (a PDF, a screenshot, or paste it), and preview it exactly as your client gets it — including from the invite sheet, before you send the link. Leave it alone and it stays the one Splyt has always asked.

Gift a character to a friend. Tap the gift button next to a character you made and pick who gets it — they get a notification, and it is theirs to race as, wearing it the moment they tap. A character is an object you own, so giving one away means you no longer have it. It costs nothing to give: you already paid when you made it.
Trainers: invite a client with a message you can make personal and send by Messages, WhatsApp, Instagram or Mail, and bring the clients you already have over in one tray.

Talking to your watch turns your phone’s music down. Tap the mic mid-workout and whatever is playing in your ears dips while you speak, with a short tone so you know it is listening — then your music comes straight back.
Trainers: outgrow three clients? Upgrade right in the app — Coach for 10 clients, Studio for 30 or Pro for 75 — and every client you train gets Splyt Pro while they’re with you.
Run a split again in one tap. A split you’ve finished has a Run again button at the top, shows clearly that it ended, and lists every time you’ve run it with the dates.
Get to your split from Add activity: the new Split button opens the one you’re running, or your splits if none is.
Training with a trainer? They’re now always one tap away on Home.

Trainers: bring the clients you already have in a couple of minutes. Drop in your spreadsheet, an export from another app, intake PDFs or screenshots of your notes — or just type who they are — and Splyt reads out every client with their goal, notes, program, rate and sessions left. Check the list, send each person your link in one tap, and when they join everything you had on them is already on their page.

Trainers get a page of their own: a link you can share anywhere with your results, how you coach, your rates and where you train. People can book or message you from it without an account, and you can feature a client’s Splyt-verified progress with their OK.

Trainers: use your own check-in form. Import the one you already send — a PDF, a photo or pasted text — start from a template, or build it. Questions Splyt can answer, like weight, steps, sleep and lifts, fill themselves in from what the client logged.

Splyt for trainers. Train clients from the app: share your link, and your roster shows who trained, who missed a planned workout, how they slept and what they owe you. Send programs, read weekly check-ins, and chat. Find it under You → Coach clients.
Training with a trainer? Join from their link, choose exactly what they can see, and their programs land on your calendar with one tap.

For trainers with Pro: a brief that has already read every client — who wrote back, who missed a session, whose sleep is sliding, who owes you — with the reply drafted. It shows the moment you open the app and stays current as clients write in. Ask the assistant anything by text or voice, and have it draft a whole program or meal plan from a client’s real data.

Meal plans. Trainers write out a client’s meals — foods, amounts, training and rest days — with calories and macros filled in for everyday foods. Clients see today’s meals on Home and tick each one ate, swapped or skipped.

Already count calories in MyFitnessPal, Cronometer or another app? Connect Apple Health from your meals and see today’s totals against your trainer’s plan. Your trainer sees the daily totals, never the foods, and a new Nutrition switch controls it.

Trainers can set their hours so clients book a session themselves, send an intake form, track supplements, set a client’s ring goals and check-in rhythm, log past sessions and payments, and group clients.
A trainer sees a client’s training calendar and today’s workout right on their page.
Send your trainer photos and files in chat — a form check, a meal plan — and long messages fold neatly.
No Apple Watch, or not wearing it every day? Your trainer sees untracked days as untracked, never as bad ones, and your check-in asks how you slept.

Your Apple Watch home screen has four corner shortcuts: today’s plan, your saved workouts, your rings and the full activity list — each one tap away instead of a few screens down. The mic is bigger and sits in the middle.

Proven splits come ready to train: every day of the split you pick has its exercises in it, chosen for you — more glute work on leg days if you’re a woman, joint-friendlier movements if you’re 50 or over.

Answer “lift together?” straight from the notification. Accept or say you can’t make it without opening anything, or tap Suggest another day to pick a different one — on your phone and, for the first time, on your watch, where the invite used to arrive with no buttons but Dismiss.

Mute one friend instead of all of them. A friend who trains twice a day used to leave you one choice — turn off every friend’s workouts — so “Mute these” on their notification is now “Mute this friend”, and only theirs go quiet. They are never told, you still see them everywhere else in Splyt, and Settings › Notifications lists who you’ve muted so you can undo it.

Share your workout on your own photo, and a whole new set of share cards — a story with your volume across it, a scoreboard of every set, a polaroid, your month as a streak, your heart rate as one glowing line, and a PR card when you set one.
Heart rate by set: under the live graph, each set of the movement you’re on shows its peak heart rate, against last time.
Log partials on your Apple Watch — tap or say “8 partials”, and they’re counted on the set.
Pick a proven split and it now comes with real workouts — Push, Pull and Legs, Upper and Lower, or the new Arnold Split — ready to train, and saved to your templates.
Attach photos when you message the founders.
During a workout, a Now row races you against your best: how much is left to beat it, and when you have.
A new look for an upcoming workout: what it is, how big it is and how long it takes up top, the movements in one tidy list, and Start always in reach at the bottom.
Open a movement in an upcoming workout to see what you lifted the last time you did that workout — and editing the plan fills in those weights and reps for you, in kg or lbs.
Touch a bar on the Trends Progress chart to read its value.
Temporary chats in Splyt AI: tap the dashed bubble at the top right and nothing you say is saved to your chats or used to update what it remembers.
Put your own photo on a leaderboard share card, then pinch and drag to frame it — with the card laid over it so you can see where everything lands.
Tap Workouts on a friend’s profile to see their workout history.

A new workout summary. How long you trained is the headline, every number sits in one place, and records come first. Each exercise is one line — tap it to see every set, with your best one lit — and the muscles you worked are named under the body map.

A friend’s day is one card now: swipe between their Splyt ring and their Apple rings, with their week following along underneath. You can leave them some encouragement right under their recent workouts.
Group pages and the Community page have been redesigned.

Forgot to stop a workout? If your heart rate came down and stayed down well before you ended it, the summary says when you most likely finished and ends it there in one tap. The same suggestion sits under the times when you edit a workout.

A day with a friend is real activities now, in order — “Back, then Basketball for 2 hours” — and it lands in both calendars as one session with the right icon on each part. Tap a chip or just type “Back” or “hoop” and that is the whole plan.
Splyt learns your gym from where you train, without ever asking. It becomes the default place for a shared session, and the invite says how far it is for the other person.
Plan a day to lift with a friend yourself. Pick any day — not only the ones Splyt suggests — and add a note so they know what to expect.
Your Splyt AI conversations live in a panel now. Open an older one, rename it, share it or delete it.
Finish setup on You: a short set of cards showing what is left to turn on, each one retiring itself once you have done it.
Say where. Search for the gym and the invite carries the place and its address — tap it to open Maps. Leaving it empty is a fine answer too.
Answer an invite with a different plan instead of a no. Change the day, the time or the place and send it back; they can agree, decline, or suggest something else again.
Lift together. Pick a friend and Splyt finds a day you can both train — the one that asks the least of either of your weeks — and lets you ask them.
A new tab bar: Home, Sharing, Stats and You, with Splyt AI as its own button beside it.
Stats, rebuilt. Totals over a range you choose, progress for each lift, a muscle radar, where you rank, leaderboards with friends — and cards to share any of it.
Reorder a live workout on your watch. Press and hold a movement, then drag it where it belongs.
Swipe right on a finished set to take it back, the same way you completed it.
The first tap of the mic shows what voice logging can do — supersets, drop sets, grips, a whole day at once.
“Add a chest-supported row after my cable row” puts it right there, not at the bottom.
Switch an exercise from your watch. On a movement’s sets, swap it for something similar without reaching for your phone — and sets you have already logged stay with the movement that earned them.

Tell the voice logger your whole day, not one workout. “Legs at 3, a run around 4, then a swim in the evening” becomes three separate workouts, each with its own activity, time and distance. Say them in any order, as vaguely as you like.
Searching to start a workout now finds your saved workouts too. Start typing a template’s name and it appears above the activity list, ready to go.
Set your grip from your watch. On a movement’s sets, tap Grip under the swap button and pick the handle, grip or width — rope, V-handle, wide bar, one arm. It shows on your phone straight away.
Picked a proven split like Push / Pull / Legs? One tap fills every day with starter exercises — sets and reps included — and you see them before anything is saved.

Stats has a new “Against your history” card: your latest session of an activity next to your last, usual and best — the same glass and heart-rate graph as during a workout — with chips to switch between the things you do most. The cramped version on the workout summary is gone.
Try Pro free for a week. Every plan now starts with a 7-day free trial — cancel any time before it ends and you are not charged.

Partials. Finished a set with half reps to failure? Add partials from the set’s menu, or just say it — “the last three sets I did partials to failure after each”. They count toward your volume at half a rep each.

Your history knows the grip. A movement’s history now includes the times you logged it under its old names (“Cable Pushdown (With Rope Attachment)” counts as Cable Pushdown on the rope), and chips at the top filter the chart, records and history to one grip.

Search for a grip — “rope pushdown”, “wide grip pull-up” — and the movement is added with that grip already picked. Saying it to the voice logger works the same way, and templates remember the grip too.

Log in kilograms. Pick it once — in Workout Defaults, or from any movement’s ⋯ menu — and everything follows: your sets, your watch, your body weight, your stats, your recaps and what Splyt AI tells you. Past workouts included. Your training is stored exactly as you logged it; only the number on screen changes.
Outside the US, Splyt now starts you in kilograms instead of pounds. Change it any time and your choice sticks.

Grips and handles. On movements like the lat pulldown, rows, curls and pushdowns, tap the V beside the name and pick how you’re doing it — wide bar, V-handle, rope, one arm — from pictures. Your “last time” weights now come from the same grip, and you can change the grip for a single set from the keypad.

Load the bar. On a barbell lift, tap the barbell on the keypad and tap the plates you’ve put on — Splyt does the math and fills in the weight. It opens already loaded with whatever you typed, so it tells you what to put on, too.
Your monthly recap now has everything the weekly one has — PRs, weight, progress photos, steps, sleep, recovery and habits — drawn week by week, with this month set against last.

Ask for your numbers from another movement — "put my leg curl weights on the leg extension" — and Splyt fills them in. You can name a movement however you say it out loud; it matches what you are already doing.
The first time you land on Home, Splyt shows you where your training calendar lives: it pulls the date down for you, holds the week open for a moment, and puts it back.
Splyt opens with a new launch animation — the wordmark splits down the middle and pulls back to your Home.
On the watch, swipe right on the rest timer to see what’s coming: your next set’s weight and reps, which set it is, and its warm-up or drop tag — or the next movement once you’ve finished one.

Copy a day on your training calendar. An empty day now has a copy button — pick a day you have already planned or trained, take the whole thing or just one activity from it, and it lands with its times.

Send your week to your trainer. The Weekly Recap now exports a full report — your training day by day, PRs, weight, steps, sleep and habits — as a PDF or a private link that opens in any browser. Choose what goes in it before you send.

Setting up Splyt is a different experience: one welcome screen with Apple or Google sign-in that remembers how you got in last time, your split built with you, and a workout that plays itself so you can see how logging works before you lift anything.
The split planner and Proven splits have been rebuilt — clearer days, clearer weeks, and scheduling that moves forward instead of dropping you back at the picker.
Correct sets you have already logged by voice. “I started with 10 pounds and then did 30 for the rest” now fixes the sets that are there instead of adding new ones underneath them.
A new account gets the Training Calendar widget free for its first week.
A template’s graph page shows your last few times doing it, so you can see the trend rather than one week of it.
Your Weekly Recap goes deeper: PRs you set, this week against last, weight, progress photos, steps, sleep, recovery and habits.
Send your week to your trainer: pick what to include, then share a link that opens in any browser, or export a PDF.
Your Apple Watch opens on a microphone. Tap it, say what you’re doing — “basketball”, “start my plan”, “rest day” — and it counts down 3-2-1 and starts. The full list is one scroll down.
Adding an activity to a workout on the watch works the same way: say “add a basketball session”.
During a rest on the watch, swipe across to control your music.
Tapping a friend’s name in your plan’s day opens what they trained.
Signing back in, the app remembers how you did it last time — Apple, Google or email — and marks that button “Last used”, so you land back in your own account instead of starting a new one.

Share a workout with anyone. Share Workout now has Copy Link, and the link rides along when you share a card — it opens your full summary as a web page, laid out exactly like the app: every set, your effort, the map, the records. No Splyt needed to see it.

Your friends’ friends. Open any friend’s profile and their friends are listed at the bottom, each with an Add button — so when one person from your gym gets on Splyt, the rest are a tap away through them.

A new Friends tab for your first day. Before you have anyone on Splyt it now leads with what friends are for, offers the people who built the app as first friends — tap either one to read their story, see their numbers and their latest session before you add them — and puts Invite friends where your thumb is.
Use these sets — paste the sets from a past session straight onto the movement you are working on.
Workout settings open from the menu during a live workout, and what you change applies right away instead of next time.
Press a bar in This Week to open that day’s sessions.

The Vessel. Swipe right from any live activity and watch a glass fill as you go, past the marks for last time, your typical and your best, with your heart rate and calories against a typical session and this week’s bars growing under it. Lifts race the weight you have moved, not the clock: a template against its own previous runs, a labelled day against days with the same label. Flip it to Graph for your heart rate over time with last time’s as a ghost.
A lift pages sideways like every other activity: your sets, then the Vessel, then your rings.
Ask the coach about a movement and it shows the movement’s card, with a tap into your history and how to do it.
The coach remembers the photo you sent. Ask “what’s it called?” a week later and it still knows.
Searching Select a workout for basketball or a sauna offers the activity list, with your search carried over. And once you type, the buttons and folders step aside so the results have the room.
With one saved workout or none, the workout picker offers Build a workout and Plan your week right there.
The home calendar hint shows a real week the way the training calendar draws one, and offers Create a split?
Mid-workout, the This Week bars answer back: press a day to read it, tap one to see the sessions behind it — what each was called, when it started, how long, how much.
Made a competition? You can now take someone out of it — Remove someone, under the cog on the race. Their score comes off the board and the race carries on.
The training calendar walks you through it the first time: where your splits live, and the plus that plans a day.
Mid-workout, searching the exercise list for an activity — a walk, basketball — offers the activity list instead of nothing.
Share a split straight from the split itself. Pick a friend and it lands under their From friends.

The live workout, redesigned. The sheet is a card tucked under the status bar; your workout’s name and the clock sit at the top with Finish and a menu beside them; every movement is its own card on a darker list, with a set’s weight and reps as “45 lbs × 6 reps” and a finished set washed in your colour. The bottom drawer is gone: a floating pill holds the mic and add, and while you rest it says how long is left — drag it sideways to change the rest, tap it for fifteen more seconds.

Say your split. Tap the mic in the split builder and describe your week — “push, pull, legs, rest, repeat, everything at 3 PM, stairs after” — and it lands as your week, days and times in place. It hears how long to run it (“for six weeks”, “until the end of October”) and when to start (“from Monday”), and weeks that differ.
Press and hold a planned workout in the training calendar and carry it to another day.
A rest day can still carry a session — a swim on your rest day — and it is still a rest day.
Tapping a movement in a workout summary opens the exercise.
Your character has its own place in Settings now, with the one you race as right there in the row. It was buried at the bottom of Appearance.
Make me. A selfie for your face, a head-to-toe photo for your build, and the outfit you want — the clothes you’re wearing or ones you describe. Animated or fully realistic. Private to you, always.
Creating a character is one thing at a time now: describe it, start from a photo, or make yourself. No more guessing whether to type and upload.
Famous faces. Describe a real person and they come out as themselves — in what they are known for, at their real height. A 7'4" centre towers over the field.
When a competition ends: how far your steps would have taken you, on a real map, with everyone on the line — and every person gets an award that is true of their week.
Race chat: a message from the group buzzes your phone, and tapping it opens the chat. Tap a photo to see it full screen, pinch to zoom, save or share it. And you can take a photo, not just pick one.
Import a whole plan at once: pick every screenshot your trainer sent in one go and they come in as one split, in order.
Swipe a saved split to delete it.
A step competition now reads your watch too, and nudges anyone whose count has gone quiet.

Reorder a split by dragging. Hold a session to move it within its day, or hold a day’s number to move the whole day — everything in it comes along. Planned Monday’s workouts and want them on Tuesday? Drag the day.

Create your own character. Describe anything — a purple bear, a lightbulb, your dog — or use a photo, see it drawn in about a minute, and a few minutes later it is yours on the road: running, swimming, lifting, cheering on the podium. Pro includes one a month.

The character library. Everything anyone has made and shared, free for everyone to use. Search it, or just browse; if someone already made what you were about to describe, Splyt offers it before you build your own.
Your workout picker, rebuilt around what you actually pick: your recent workouts first, search at the top, and one tap to start anything.
When you pick a time to train, Splyt now tells you the hour you usually train — and says something if that time collides with your sleep.
Splits have a home of their own. Open the training calendar and tap the grid to pick a proven split, sorted by how many days a week you can train, or build one by hand.
Splits can roll instead of repeating on weekdays. Four days on, one off keeps going round whatever day it lands on, so your week no longer has to be seven days long.
Generating a split now asks properly: which days work best, what you want to bring up, and what hurts and how. Injuries get the movement swapped rather than the day skipped.
Review what a split puts on your calendar before it puts it there.
The competition widget is free for everyone. Put your race on your home screen whether or not you are on Pro.
Get a notification when somebody joins a group competition you are in, so the standings never quietly grow a name you do not recognise.
Swap one activity of a planned day without rebuilding the whole day.

See a friend’s training week from your own calendar. Tap the avatar in the Training Calendar header and pick anyone you are friends with — their planned and completed days, read-only. It used to mean leaving your calendar, finding their profile and opening theirs.

A setting for whether your phone alerts you when a rest period ends while you are wearing your watch. On by default — a wrist buzz is easy to miss under a working set, and a watch cannot put a sound in the headphones you already have on.

Your Apple Watch counts reps on lat pulldowns and straight-arm pulldowns. Pull-ups and chin-ups are deliberately left out — there your hands stay fixed to the bar and your body moves past them, so there is nothing at the wrist to count.

The founders can now start a conversation with you. Until now that chat only worked one way — you had to write first. If we message you it arrives like any other notification, and tapping it opens the chat so you can just reply.

Any saved workout can now be sent as a link. Whoever opens it sees the whole workout — every set, the weights and reps, your warm-up and top sets, supersets round by round, drop sets and rests, and any note you left on a movement — in a page that works without Splyt and without an account. Share a workout from your Saved tab and the link is what gets sent.
If they already have Splyt, the link opens straight into the app on the workout, ready to save to their own library.
Pick a light or dark style for a workout recap before you post it.

Planning a split now starts by picking its shape. Six common weeks — full body, upper/lower, push/pull/legs and more — each drawn day by day with the muscles it trains, so you can choose by looking. Pick one and the week fills in with named days you can then build however you like, or start from a blank week as before.

Tapping a notification about a friend’s gym trip now opens the whole trip as one session — the lift, the sauna and the jacuzzi together, with the totals for all of it — instead of whichever single part the link pointed at.
Hold a message in a competition chat to report it or block whoever sent it.

When somebody leaves a competition you are in, you are told — and if they were the last one racing you, the standings say so and offer to bring somebody else in or close it out. Anyone who has left is now listed under the board, so a race that gets quieter explains itself.
You can leave a one-on-one competition too. Because a versus cannot carry on with one person, leaving retires it for both of you and lets the other person know.

A competition that hasn’t started yet opens on its own fight card — everyone who is in it, stood up together with the date underneath, instead of an empty race with the whole field sat on zero. Works for a group and for a one-on-one, where it bills the matchup.
Accept or decline a competition invite straight from the notification, on your phone or your watch, without opening the app.
You can leave a group competition you joined. Your score comes off the board and the race carries on without you.

The competition map shows who is training right now. On a lifting competition it also shows what they have put up so far in the session — kept separate from the leaderboard, which still only counts workouts you have finished.
You can add a friend to a competition without sending them a link. If they are already on Splyt, put them straight in.
Hold a message in a competition chat to report it or block the person who sent it.

A group competition invite now waits for your answer. Accept and Decline actually do something — until you accept you are not on the start line, and the standings list who was invited and has not replied yet instead of showing them at zero, which read as losing badly rather than as not playing.

Step competitions you can watch. A race against your friends now runs in a world — a road, a gym, a pool — with a character you pick and can change. Your steps move you along it, and the map replays what happened while you were away.
A run, ride or swim competition is won on distance, not on how many sessions you logged. Three short jogs no longer beat one long run.
Two people get a head-to-head instead of a leaderboard, and a finished race opens on its result and tells you when it ended.
Invite links show the race itself — who is asking, what the competition is, and when it actually runs — instead of a bare link.
A competition widget and a multi-habit widget for your home screen.
You can attach screenshots to feedback, so a bug you can see is a bug you can show.
A brand-new account is offered the founders as a first friend, instead of an empty Friends tab.

Your weekly and monthly recaps now show the training calendar itself — the week laid out the way it reads everywhere else in the app, instead of a separate summary that had to be matched up in your head.
Previewing a workout someone shared with you shows the workout, not a summary of it.

Bring your training history over from Strong or Hevy. Export from the other app and share it straight into Splyt, or pick the file yourself from Profile → Import Data. Splyt shows you what it found — how many workouts, over what dates, which movements are new to you — before anything is added, and every session lands on the day you actually trained.
Imported workouts count. They sit on their real dates in your training calendar and feed your stats, records and totals like anything you logged here yourself.

Changed your mind? Profile → Import Data → Last import lists everything you’ve brought in, from which app, with every workout it added — and undoes any one of them on its own. Undoing what came from Strong leaves what came from Hevy exactly where it is.

Share the shape of your run. An outdoor run, ride or walk now leads its share gallery with a Route card — distance, pace and time over the trace of where you went, on a clear background so you can drop it straight onto your own photo of the place. Pick the line’s colour; it starts on your accent.

Call off a planned session from the editor you opened it in. Remove one activity from a day that holds several, or take the whole session off the day — and for a repeating plan, choose whether it’s just this day or every one from here on.
Pick how your home Activity section reads. Settings → Home View → Activity Layout: grouped by type with a total per kind, or one list in the order things happened. Grouped stays the default.
Editing a planned activity now opens the same builder you use to make a template — pick movements, set reps and weights, superset and reorder — and you can change the day and time without leaving it.

Your weekly and monthly recaps break the week down by what you actually did — how many lifts, and how long you spent on cardio, sport and recovery. A kind you did not do that week simply is not listed.
Share your whole day, not just one workout. Open your ring from the home screen and Share Day builds the same cards a finished workout gets, for everything you did.
Share a single activity out of a grouped session — the sauna on its own, not the lift it followed.
Move a whole planned session to another day in one go. Every activity in it keeps its own time.
Your day’s activity is grouped by what kind of thing it was — Strength, Cardio, Sports and Recovery — each with its own total, and the whole day’s total beside the Activity heading.
Did the same thing more than once? It folds into a single row you can tap open to see each session. Workouts stay listed on their own, since each already has its own name.
Read a friend’s workout history — tap the name at the top of History to switch whose sessions you are looking at, the same way you switch whose recap you read on Stats.
Plan a workout straight from the + on your home screen, instead of going out to the workout picker.
